resources.string: Rest without guilt
If your body has less energy today, resting a bit more is okay. Lighten your plans where you can.
Warmth can help
For some people, a hot water bottle or a warm shower feels good during their period. See what works for you.
Stay hydrated
Drinking water and warm drinks throughout the day may help you feel better.
Say what you need
If you need help or more space today, telling the people close to you can make things easier.
Everyone\'s experience differs
Flow and length can vary from person to person, and even from month to month. There is no need to compare.
Gentle movement, if you like
Some people feel better after a short walk or gentle stretching. If you\'re not up for it, resting is a good choice too.
Log your symptoms
Logging symptoms over a few cycles helps you learn your own patterns and talk to a doctor more clearly if needed.
Take strong pain seriously
If pain is strong enough to disrupt your daily life, it\'s a good idea to talk with a doctor or health professional.
A good time for small starts
Some people notice more energy in these days. If you do too, it might be a nice time to start a small habit.
Give yourself credit
Notice what you\'ve done this week, even the small things. Paying attention to progress feels good.
Plan something together
If you\'d like, plan an activity or a date with your partner for the coming days.
Regular meals
Regular, varied meals can help keep your energy steady. They don\'t have to be perfect, just regular.
Movement you enjoy
If you feel like it, try a physical activity you enjoy: something fun, not an obligation.
What is the follicular phase?
It usually runs from the end of your period until around ovulation. Its length varies between people, which is one reason cycle lengths differ.
Time for yourself
Set aside a little time just for you: a book, music, or anything that calms you.
An estimated window, not a fixed day
Kenaret only shows an estimated ovulation window. The real timing can differ, and this app is not a method of contraception.
Body signals
Some people notice changes in discharge or in how their body feels around now, and some notice nothing. Both are normal.
Regular sleep
Try to keep a regular sleep schedule. Good sleep affects your energy and mood across the whole cycle.
Open conversation
If something about your body or your relationship is on your mind, a calm and honest talk with your partner can help.
Accept how you feel today
However you feel today is valid. You don\'t have to match any particular idea of this phase.
A short walk
If you have a moment, a few minutes walking outside can refresh your day.
Plan a lighter week
For some people the days before a period feel heavier. If that\'s true for you, plan a lighter schedule ahead of time.
Get ready ahead
Keep the things you usually need for your period within reach now, so you\'re not caught off guard.
Be kinder to yourself
If you have less patience these days, go easy on yourself. Everyone\'s experience is different, and every feeling is valid.
Notice salt and caffeine
Some people find that less salt or caffeine in these days eases bloating or restlessness. See how it is for you.
Tell them in advance
If you know what helps you in the coming days, share it with your partner ahead of time so they don\'t have to guess.
Enough sleep
Some people need more sleep around now. If you can, go to bed a little earlier.
Mood notes
Writing a few lines about how you feel can lighten your mind and later show you your own patterns.
What is the luteal phase?
It usually runs from after ovulation until the next period. Symptoms differ for everyone, and some people have none at all.
When changes feel big
If symptoms before your period strongly affect daily life, talking with a doctor or health professional can help.
Ask, don\'t guess
Instead of guessing how she feels, ask her: “What would help you today?”
Small everyday tasks
Volunteer for something small, like making a warm drink, doing the dishes or the daily shopping.
Supplies
If getting certain things is harder for her these days, you can offer to help. Just ask first what she needs.
Take pain seriously
If she says she\'s in pain, believe her and don\'t downplay it. Simply being there often matters more than any solution.
Room to rest
If she\'s tired, make room for rest: keep things calm or take over some tasks yourself.
Every experience is different
Periods differ between people and even from month to month. What helped last month might not be needed this month.
Skip period jokes
Jokes about periods or symptoms, even well-meant ones, can feel hurtful. Respect is always the safer choice.
Keep plans flexible
If you had plans and she isn\'t feeling up to it, offer to postpone or simplify without making it a big deal.
Time together
If you\'re both up for it, plan an activity or a date together. Ask her what she\'d enjoy.
Back her plans
If she\'s starting a new goal or project, show interest and ask how you can support her.
The follicular phase
This phase usually follows the period. Some people feel more energetic, but not everyone does. Don\'t assume, ask.
Unhurried talks
Make time for a calm, unhurried conversation about her day, her plans or anything she wants to talk about.
Share chores fairly
Support isn\'t only for period days. Sharing housework fairly all month long is real partnership.
Show appreciation
A simple word of appreciation for something she did, or for who she is, can brighten her day.
The cycle is more than the period
The menstrual cycle has several phases, and the period is only one of them. Understanding the whole cycle builds empathy.
Only an estimate
Kenaret shows only an estimated ovulation window. It is not reliable for preventing pregnancy.
Respect choices
Decisions about bodies and intimacy are shared and need full consent from both of you. Always ask and respect the answer.
Don\'t assume
No phase decides how she feels. Hear about her day from her, not from a calendar.
A small surprise
Something small and unexpected, like her favourite meal or a kind note, can feel lovely.
Active listening
When she talks, put your phone down and really listen. You don\'t always need to offer a solution.
Every body is different
Some people notice changes around now and some don\'t notice any. Curiosity beats conclusions.
One simple question
Today you could start with a simple question: “Is there anything I can help with?”
Don\'t judge
If her mood is different, don\'t judge it or blame hormones. Every feeling has its own reasons.
Prepare ahead
If her period may be coming soon, ask whether there\'s anything she\'d like to have ready.
Lighten the mental load
Fully take over a few planned tasks, like shopping or paying bills, so she has less to keep track of.
Personal space
If she needs personal space, respect it. Taking some time alone doesn\'t mean something is wrong between you.
Handle disagreements calmly
If you disagree, focus on the issue itself and avoid lines like “It must be your period.”
The luteal phase
This phase usually falls between ovulation and the next period. Some people have symptoms like tiredness or bloating, others have none.
Restful sleep
If she needs more sleep, keep things quiet or handle the morning tasks yourself.
Being there matters
Sometimes the best support is just being there: a film together, a warm tea, or sitting side by side in silence.
